extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal financial assistance (educational institutions), Title IX stakeholders, commenters, and legal practitioners involved in Title IX rulemaking and implementation
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to the Department of Education's Title IX final regulations responding to public comments; explains legal authority, procedural choices, scope, effective date, and implementation guidance for recipients and commenters. It clarifies how the Department interpreted comments and why it adopted or rejected suggested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the religious exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's religious exemption applies to educational institutions controlled by a religious organization, but it does not exempt student organizations, individual employees or students, or educational institutions not controlled by religious organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges concerns about speech conflicts with First Amendment rights but states that nothing in the final regulations requires or authorizes a recipient to infringe on individuals' First Amendment or other constitutional rights (consistent with §106.6(d)(1)). The interplay between the prohibition on sex-based harassment and First Amendment rights is addressed under the definition of sex-based harassment in §106.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment noninfringement principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations requires or authorizes a recipient to infringe on individuals' First Amendment or other constitutional rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department points to §106.6(d)(1) and directs readers to the discussion of sex-based harassment definition (§106.2) for how tensions between harassment prohibitions and free speech are handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 34 CFR 75.500(d) and 76.500(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions prohibiting public postsecondary institutions receiving Department grants from enforcing certain non-discrimination policies against religious student organizations were not addressed in this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department did not request comments on these regulations in the July 2022 NPRM because they were outside this rulemaking's scope; the Department has proposed rescinding them in a separate rulemaking (see 88 FR 10857).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated rulemaking not required for Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements of section 492 of the Higher Education Act (HEA) for negotiated rulemaking apply only to regulations implementing Title IV of the HEA and do not apply to Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required to conduct negotiated rulemaking for Title IX, the Department solicited live and written comments (June 2021 Title IX Public Hearing), conducted listening sessions, and considered recommendations from practitioners and experts among the hundreds of thousands of comments on the July 2022 NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public hearings, listening sessions, and notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department used public hearings, listening sessions, and the notice-and-comment process to solicit input from affected entities and individuals prior to issuing the proposed regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations from practitioners and experts were among the comments received; comments are posted on Regulations.gov. The Department coordinated with other agencies (OMB) and obtained review/approval from DOJ under Executive Orders 12866 and 12250.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory group creation discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to create a standing advisory group to implement the final regulations because the public hearing, listening sessions, and notice-and-comment process provided sufficient opportunity for input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in the final regulations precludes recipients from creating their own advisory groups; the Department will offer technical assistance as appropriate to promote compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate notices for interrelated proposals are permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing two separate notices of proposed rulemaking to amend the Title IX regulations did not deprive the public of proper notice and opportunity to consider interrelated interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The July 2022 NPRM made clear that proposed §106.31(a)(2) would not apply in the athletics eligibility context and that a separate notice (Athletics NPRM) would follow; the Department intends to publish separate final regulations related to sex-related eligibility criteria for male and female athletic teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency review and compliance with Executive Orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department coordinated review of proposed regulations with OMB and had the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights at DOJ review and approve publication to satisfy Executive Orders 12866 and 12250.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interagency review provided other federal agencies that administer Title IX enforcement an opportunity to review and comment before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful opportunity to comment and comment period length
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, agencies must give interested persons an opportunity to participate; case law generally interprets this to require a meaningful opportunity to comment and typically not less than 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department provided a 60-day comment period on the July 2022 NPRM, which it finds sufficient and declines to extend; the Department received over 240,000 comments, which it views as evidence of meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations.gov submission, posting, and redaction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When a commenter submits on Regulations.gov they receive a tracking number; the Department posted comments publicly except for (1) portions containing personally identifiable information about someone other than the commenter and (2) comments containing threats of harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Regulations.gov system allows commenters to self-report representing multiple individuals; the Department corrected an erroneous self-reported count. The Department accepted alternate submission methods for those who requested accommodations and consulted GSA regarding reported submission difficulties. Posted comments containing third‑party PII were redacted; review for posting caused occasional lags between submission and public posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of comment tallies and non-removal of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no loss of comments; an erroneous self-reported number by a single commenter inflated counts and was corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSA generates comment tallies on Regulations.gov; the Department and GSA did not eliminate comments or types of comments except for the two narrow exceptions consistent with Department policy (PII and threats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date minimum and retroactivity prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the APA, the effective date cannot be fewer than 30 days after publication unless special circumstances apply; agencies may create retroactive regulations only when expressly authorized by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department set the effective date of the final regulations to August 1, 2024 (more than 90 days after publication) to give recipients ample time to comply; the Department will not enforce these regulations retroactively and will evaluate conduct before the effective date under the statute and regulations in effect when the alleged conduct occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition and technical assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may need technical assistance during the transition between publication and the effective date and after the regulations become effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will offer technical assistance as appropriate to promote compliance and notes the effective date coincides with summer break to help recipients finalize policies and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prevention training requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to provide student-facing prevention or sex-education programming beyond §106.8(d), which relates to individuals responsible for implementing the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Department does not control school curricula, it will not add mandates about instruction to students; nothing in the final regulations precludes recipients from using their discretion to provide educational programming. Funding for such prevention programming lies with Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth Amendment and federalism limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not violate the Tenth Amendment; the Federal Government retains authority to regulate sex discrimination in education programs or activities that receive Federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's position (from the 2020 amendments) is that recipients who accept federal funds agree to comply with Title IX and implementing regulations as a condition of those funds; the regulations are consistent with the Tenth Amendment as they do not compel States but regulate recipients of Federal assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority to promulgate Title IX regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have delegated authority under 20 U.S.C. 1682 to effectuate Title IX (20 U.S.C. 1681) by issuing rules, regulations, or orders of general applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This authority includes ensuring compliance by termination or refusal to continue assistance; prohibiting sex-based harassment and requiring remedies to eliminate harm and prevent recurrence falls within that delegated authority. The regulations implement, not amend, Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to require remedies for complainants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has authority to require recipients to provide remedies to complainants because such remedies eliminate harm and prevent recurrence of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring remedies is part of effectuating Title IX under 20 U.S.C. 1682 and is consistent with judicial precedent recognizing sexual harassment as sex discrimination under Title IX (Gebser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for disqualifying agency officials from rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency member should be disqualified only when there has been a clear and convincing showing that the agency member has an 'unalterably closed mind' on matters critical to the disposition of the proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past advocacy or policy statements by Assistant Secretary Lhamon do not, by themselves, show disqualifying bias; statements made before adoption of proposed rulemaking or before assuming office do not demonstrate an inability to engage in reasoned decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory justification and evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies comply with Executive Orders (e.g., 12866, 14021) by identifying problems and assessing significance; agencies are not required to produce empirical evidence and may adopt prophylactic rules to prevent potential problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department relied on federal case law, enforcement experience, stakeholder feedback, and qualitative benefits (such as psychological wellbeing improvements) in the Regulatory Impact Analysis to justify regulatory action; limited quantitative data does not preclude agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of qualitative benefits in regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative measures of benefits (e.g., psychological wellbeing) are essential to consider under Executive Order 12866 and OMB guidance (Circular A-4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department relied on qualitative benefits where quantitative datasets were limited and included those assessments in the Regulatory Impact Analysis to support the need for regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for durable, stable regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested long-lasting regulations that reduce uncertainty caused by shifting Title IX regulatory landscapes; time and resources are required when regulations change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes concerns about frequently changing regulations and their practical burdens (updating policies, training), but did not adopt specific additional measures in response to this comment in this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate athletics rulemaking authority and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Athletics present unique considerations; the Department issued a separate Athletics NPRM and intends to publish separate final regulations related to sex-related eligibility criteria for male and female athletic teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department maintains authority under the Javits Amendment to promulgate reasonable provisions governing athletics that consider the nature of particular sports; it received over 150,000 comments on the Athletics NPRM and will treat athletics rulemaking separately to ensure full consideration.
